| You can make the difference.
Hi Derek, this is Roy Cooper.
I don’t mess around with something as important as representing the people of North Carolina, Derek.
Every race I’ve ever run, I’ve been in it to win — even when the odds seemed long. You’ve been there with me every time, and together, we’ve succeeded. Now, this election for the U.S. Senate may be our toughest challenge yet. **[So when I ask you to split a donation between our campaign and Adam Schiff, it’s because your contribution could make the difference between victory and defeat.](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/1014?c0=abs-em-cooper25.C4cz3v&refcode=AU_ABS_FR_TAN_GEN_AC_20251228_PM1_V1_S1&email=&t=3&akid=9343%2E5257348%2EHEKf88)**

I will always be straightforward about this campaign: our plans, where we stand in the polls, what we expect to come, and what we need from you.
Right now, we’re preparing for national GOP money groups to spend _hundreds of millions_ against us, and Democrats are being outraised by Republicans. Meanwhile, various polls have shown either a dead heat or us with a slight lead.

Hi Peter,

Early in my career, Bernie Sanders gave me a piece of advice I’ve never
forgotten.

He said, “In politics, people succeed either by being really good at lying
or really good at telling the truth. You strike me as someone who’s not
good at lying — so your job is to get really good at telling the truth.”

So today, I’m going to tell you some truths about our campaign.

We’re statistically tied with our MAGA Republican opponent. We have the
momentum to win.

December 31st marks our biggest fundraising hurdle yet — our final FEC
deadline of the year.

This is, no exaggeration, a make-or-break moment for our campaign.

In just a couple of days, we need to raise as much as we can to prove that
a people-powered campaign — one that rejects AIPAC and corporate PAC money
— has enough resources to take on the would-be oligarchs and win.

Finally, one more piece of truth: I don’t love asking people for money.

But because this is a 100% people-powered campaign, I’m relying on folks
like you who care about the future of our party and our country to pitch

**December 28, 2025** **SUNDAY NEWS DIGEST**
| | Dear Rocky Mountain Voice family,
As we close out the year, we wanted to pause and reflect on what this community — and this newsroom — has spent the last two years doing here in Colorado.
Rocky Mountain Voice was never built to chase headlines or jump from controversy to controversy. A lot of our most important reporting this year came from sticking with stories long after they stopped being fashionable, or after other outlets decided they were “settled.”
That’s what today’s featured piece is about: **[Boots on the Ground, Uncovering Colorado’s Hidden Truths](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
Over the past two years, we’ve spent a lot of time doing the unglamorous work — pulling public records, talking to people who didn’t feel safe speaking publicly, and following threads that didn’t fit cleanly into a news cycle. In many cases, if we hadn’t kept asking questions, those stories simply would’ve disappeared.
What’s also worth saying out loud: many of our most-read stories this year didn’t come from professional reporters at all. They came from citizen journalists — parents, ranchers, energy workers, teachers, and everyday Coloradans who saw something happening in their community and were willing to speak up.
Some of our most impactful coverage this year came from that approach — whether it was the Tina Peters case, election-related transparency issues, energy and land-use policies affecting families and small producers, or education stories that parents felt weren’t being taken seriously elsewhere. These weren’t always easy stories to cover, but they were stories people here in Colorado kept asking about. Many of these pieces went on to become our **[most-read and most-shared stories of the year.](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
We encourage you to read today’s article and take some time with our [top stories of the year.](https://link.email.joinrmv.) They give a good snapshot of what we’ve been focused on — and what we think still matters going forward.
And as we head into the new year, stay tuned. This week’s newsletters will include a few more looks back at 2025 and some reflections as we officially enter 2026 on Thursday. There’s more context we want to share, and more ground we plan to cover.
Thank you for reading, sharing, and supporting independent journalism in Colorado. This work continues because you’ve decided it matters.
— Team RMV

**[After the pardon: The constitutional question Colorado courts now face](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) President Donald Trump’s pardon of Tina Peters did not end her case. It changed it. What now sits before Colorado’s courts is no longer a question of guilt or innocence, nor even whether Peters should remain imprisoned while her appeal moves forward. The unresolved issue is more fundamental than that: whether the state still has authority to proceed in light of a federal pardon.
**[From question to confrontation: Peters’ legal team forces Colorado courts to choose](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) One day after the constitutional question facing Colorado courts came into focus, attorneys for former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters moved to force an answer. Late Tuesday, Peters’ legal team filed an urgent motion asking the Colorado Court of Appeals to determine whether it still has jurisdiction to proceed at all, given a presidential pardon and what her attorneys argue are unresolved violations of federal election law. __
**[Lawmakers demand Polis reverse electrification push after shutoffs](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) Colorado lawmakers are pressing Gov. Jared Polis to reverse course on electrification after recent power shutoffs raised fresh concerns about grid reliability and public safety. “We write to express grave concerns over your administration’s aggressive push for statewide unfunded electrification mandates,” the lawmakers wrote in a Dec. 23 letter. __

**STATE**
**[Colorado Congressman Accuses Polis Administration Of Mismanaging Road Funds](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**[FOX 31 NEWS](https://link.email.joinrmv.) A Colorado congressman is accusing the state of mismanaging transportation dollars, arguing that despite record funding, roads across Colorado are in worse shape than ever. Rep. Gabe Evans, who represents Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, shared an exclusive letter with FOX31 that he is sending directly to Gov. Jared Polis and Colorado Department of Transportation Executive Director Shoshana Lew.

**[Court Halts Colorado Effort to Mandate Gas Stove Health Warnings](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**[COMPLETE COLORADO](https://link.email.joinrmv.) A federal judge on Friday sided with an appliance manufacturing trade group in pausing enforcement of a Colorado law requiring consumer warning labels on gas stove appliances. Plaintiffs see the ruling as a win against state compelled speech, albeit a temporary one, as the litigation will likely continue.
**[Colorado Risks $24M in Federal Funds as thousands of Commercial Driver’s Licenses Were Issued Illegally](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**[DENVER7](https://link.email.joinrmv.) The head of the U.S. Department of Transportation threatened Monday to withhold $24 million in federal funding from the state of Colorado for what he described as a slow response to a major violation of federal commercial driver’s license regulations.

**NATIONAL**
**[From fracture to formation: What AmericaFest revealed about the next generation](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) I arrived late to the Young Conservatives of Colorado happy hour on Saturday night, nearly an hour after it had begun. The happy hour was already winding down in an outdoor hotel lounge in Phoenix. A small circle of college students and recent grads sat around a fireplace after a full day at Turning Point USA’s AmericaFest. Some were holding drinks. The tone was relaxed amid laughter, but not rowdy.

**[Why two House bills on medical transition procedures produced different votes](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY JEN SCHUMANN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) The U.S. House passed two bills this month aimed at restricting federal involvement in medical transition procedures for minors. They used different enforcement tools. And they produced different voting coalitions.

**[Republicans Should Just Say No To Josh Hawley’s Crusade Against Data Centers](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY BOOKER LIGHTMAN, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) _The Data center boom is creating a political conundrum for Republicans, or so Politico would have you believe. For while President Trump and the large majority of Republican elected officials are in favor of data centers, Josh Hawley, Marjorie Taylor Greene, and Thomas Massie stand in opposition to the Trump administration.

**[Federal Civil Rights Complaint Accuses Cherry Creek Schools of Race-Based Discipline and Retaliation](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY SHAINA COLE, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) A federal civil-rights complaint now puts Cherry Creek School District under scrutiny over allegations of race-based discrimination and retaliation. In its press release, America First Legal says Cherry Creek has “branded student misconduct ‘culturally appropriate’ and blocked discipline based on race,” claiming the district has replaced equal treatment with an unlawful double standard. __
**[Fort Lewis College Student Stands Firm After Turning Point USA Chapter Sparks Backlash](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**[COLORADO POLITICS](https://link.email.joinrmv.) Before Fort Lewis College senior Jonah Flynn became president of the newly formed FLC Turning Point USA chapter, he described himself as a liberal-leaning atheist. Flynn, a senior studying philosophy and Spanish, gained local and national attention after the Associated Students of Fort Lewis College initially denied his request to start a Turning Point chapter at an Oct. 29 meeting.
**[Colorado Hockey Mom Says Whistleblowing Sparked Retaliation and Legal Threats](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**[USA TODAY](https://link.email.joinrmv.) For months, Brooke Wilfley raised concerns that the president of her local youth hockey governing board was using his position for profit. The Denver-area hockey mom discovered that the president, Randy Kanai, was secretly routing the Colorado Amateur Hockey Association’s money through his private company.

**COMMENTARY**
**[Good News or Fake News — Love: The News That Changes Everything](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY DRAKE HUNTER, [ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) _Hope taught us patience. Peace showed us strength. Joy revealed how to move forward. Now, as we conclude our Advent Series, we focus on its core: Love. Not the sentimental version. Not the weaponized form. Not the diluted kind sold by culture, commerce, or clicks. Instead, love with meaning._
__
**[When Christmas came under fire: Remembering Bastogne](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**
**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)**[GROUNDS FOR TRUTH](https://link.email.joinrmv.) _It’s easy to romanticize Christmas during wartime—the carols echoing through snow-covered fields, soldiers sharing a quiet moment of peace amid the chaos. But for the men of the 101st Airborne Division hunkered down in Bastogne, Belgium, in December 1944, the holiday was a raw test of endurance, grit, and unshakeable faith._

**[](https://link.email.joinrmv.)** BY DRAKE HUNTER,[ ROCKY MOUNTAIN VOICE](https://link.email.joinrmv.) _As I write these words, Sherrie and I are again in the hospital, where we’ve spent the past 22 days experiencing a whirlwind of emotions and events. Each day presents new challenges—tests, treatments, setbacks, and small wins. The breathtaking sunrises over the Rocky Mountains seen from the hospital window serve as a constant reminder of hope._

clean_body: Looking Back on the Stories That Mattered This Year | | | | December 28, 2025 SUNDAY NEWS DIGEST | | Dear Rocky Mountain Voice family, As we close out the year, we wanted to pause and reflect on what this community — and this newsroom — has spent the last two years doing here in Colorado. Rocky Mountain Voice was never built to chase headlines or jump from controversy to controversy. A lot of our most important reporting this year came from sticking with stories long after they stopped being fashionable, or after other outlets decided they were “settled.” That’s what today’s featured piece is about: Over the past two years, we’ve spent a lot of time doing the unglamorous work — pulling public records, talking to people who didn’t feel safe speaking publicly, and following threads that didn’t fit cleanly into a news cycle. In many cases, if we hadn’t kept asking questions, those stories simply would’ve disappeared. What’s also worth saying out loud: many of our most-read stories this year didn’t come from professional reporters at all. They came from citizen journalists — parents, ranchers, energy workers, teachers, and everyday Coloradans who saw something happening in their community and were willing to speak up. Some of our most impactful coverage this year came from that approach — whether it was the Tina Peters case, election-related transparency issues, energy and land-use policies affecting families and small producers, or education stories that parents felt weren’t being taken seriously elsewhere. These weren’t always easy stories to cover, but they were stories people here in Colorado kept asking about. Many of these pieces went on to become our We encourage you to read today’s article and take some time with our They give a good snapshot of what we’ve been focused on — and what we think still matters going forward. And as we head into the new year, stay tuned. This week’s newsletters will include a few more looks back at 2025 and some reflections as we officially enter 2026 on Thursday. There’s more context we want to share, and more ground we plan to cover. Thank you for reading, sharing, and supporting independent journalism in Colorado. This work continues because you’ve decided it matters. — Team RMV | | | | | TOP STORIES OF THE WEEK BY JEN SCHUMANN, President Donald Trump’s pardon of Tina Peters did not end her case. It changed it. What now sits before Colorado’s courts is no longer a question of guilt or innocence, nor even whether Peters should remain imprisoned while her appeal moves forward. The unresolved issue is more fundamental than that: whether the state still has authority to proceed in light of a federal pardon. BY JEN SCHUMANN, One day after the constitutional question facing Colorado courts came into focus, attorneys for former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters moved to force an answer. Late Tuesday, Peters’ legal team filed an urgent motion asking the Colorado Court of Appeals to determine whether it still has jurisdiction to proceed at all, given a presidential pardon and what her attorneys argue are unresolved violations of federal election law. BY JEN SCHUMANN, Colorado lawmakers are pressing Gov. Jared Polis to reverse course on electrification after recent power shutoffs raised fresh concerns about grid reliability and public safety. “We write to express grave concerns over your administration’s aggressive push for statewide unfunded electrification mandates,” the lawmakers wrote in a Dec. 23 letter. | STATE A Colorado congressman is accusing the state of mismanaging transportation dollars, arguing that despite record funding, roads across Colorado are in worse shape than ever. Rep. Gabe Evans, who represents Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, shared an exclusive letter with FOX31 that he is sending directly to Gov. Jared Polis and Colorado Department of Transportation Executive Director Shoshana Lew. A federal judge on Friday sided with an appliance manufacturing trade group in pausing enforcement of a Colorado law requiring consumer warning labels on gas stove appliances. Plaintiffs see the ruling as a win against state compelled speech, albeit a temporary one, as the litigation will likely continue. The head of the U.S. Department of Transportation threatened Monday to withhold $24 million in federal funding from the state of Colorado for what he described as a slow response to a major violation of federal commercial driver’s license regulations. | NATIONAL BY JEN SCHUMANN, I arrived late to the Young Conservatives of Colorado happy hour on Saturday night, nearly an hour after it had begun. The happy hour was already winding down in an outdoor hotel lounge in Phoenix. A small circle of college students and recent grads sat around a fireplace after a full day at Turning Point USA’s AmericaFest. Some were holding drinks. The tone was relaxed amid laughter, but not rowdy. BY JEN SCHUMANN, The U.S. House passed two bills this month aimed at restricting federal involvement in medical transition procedures for minors. They used different enforcement tools. And they produced different voting coalitions. BY BOOKER LIGHTMAN, The Data center boom is creating a political conundrum for Republicans, or so Politico would have you believe. For while President Trump and the large majority of Republican elected officials are in favor of data centers, Josh Hawley, Marjorie Taylor Greene, and Thomas Massie stand in opposition to the Trump administration. | LOCAL BY SHAINA COLE, A federal civil-rights complaint now puts Cherry Creek School District under scrutiny over allegations of race-based discrimination and retaliation. In its press release, America First Legal says Cherry Creek has “branded student misconduct ‘culturally appropriate’ and blocked discipline based on race,” claiming the district has replaced equal treatment with an unlawful double standard. Before Fort Lewis College senior Jonah Flynn became president of the newly formed FLC Turning Point USA chapter, he described himself as a liberal-leaning atheist. Flynn, a senior studying philosophy and Spanish, gained local and national attention after the Associated Students of Fort Lewis College initially denied his request to start a Turning Point chapter at an Oct. 29 meeting. For months, Brooke Wilfley raised concerns that the president of her local youth hockey governing board was using his position for profit. The Denver-area hockey mom discovered that the president, Randy Kanai, was secretly routing the Colorado Amateur Hockey Association’s money through his private company. | COMMENTARY BY DRAKE HUNTER, Hope taught us patience. Peace showed us strength. Joy revealed how to move forward. Now, as we conclude our Advent Series, we focus on its core: Love. Not the sentimental version. Not the weaponized form. Not the diluted kind sold by culture, commerce, or clicks. Instead, love with meaning. It’s easy to romanticize Christmas during wartime—the carols echoing through snow-covered fields, soldiers sharing a quiet moment of peace amid the chaos. But for the men of the 101st Airborne Division hunkered down in Bastogne, Belgium, in December 1944, the holiday was a raw test of endurance, grit, and unshakeable faith. BY HEIDI GANAHL, Rocky Mountain Voice has spent the last two years covering stories that don’t fit neatly into a news cycle. We’ve reported on fraud, government overreach, and policy failures by doing the unglamorous work — pulling records, talking to whistleblowers, and sticking with stories long after other outlets lost interest. BY DRAKE HUNTER, As I write these words, Sherrie and I are again in the hospital, where we’ve spent the past 22 days experiencing a whirlwind of emotions and events. Each day presents new challenges—tests, treatments, setbacks, and small wins. body:
If you take one lesson away from 2025, let it be this:
| [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/122145246/591751208/-3547583?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9FQS9FQTAxMy8xLzg5Mjk0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjljODRhNzE0LTVjZTQtZjAxMS04MTk1LTAwMGQzYTFkNThhYSIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=gNIjIkWLtk6b5qeWXLv_FAa6fIvAFVuu_TJPxdX_Bvo=&emci=d78fb2cf-72e2-f011-8195-000d3a1d58aa&emdi=9c84a714-5ce4-f011-8195-000d3a1d58aa&ceid=8431045)
---

Peter, American democracy has been put through a gauntlet in 2025. It started with Republicans in North Carolina trying to overturn the result of a free and fair election for state supreme court. Thanks to people like you, democracy ultimately prevailed. Then powerful right-wing interests, including Elon Musk, spent millions to try to buy a seat on the Wisconsin Supreme Court and flip the balance of power. Our movement fought back, and won the day. But we continue to face existential, anti-democracy threats. Conservatives have petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court to effectively strike down the Voting Rights Act and upend the voting power of communities of color in America. We anxiously await that ruling. And throughout the last five months, Republicans have thrust the nation into a shameful redistricting crisis orchestrated by the Trump White House. They’re trying to rig the outcome of the midterm elections so they can’t lose. The ultimate outcome of their cynical power grab remains up in the air. A lot remains uncertain, but if you take one lesson away from the past year, let it be this: Some folks on the other side want you to believe they’re all-powerful. They want you to be dispirited and pessimistic about our future. But we’ve seen time and again that it’s a lie. When we organize, when we stand up for justice, when we show some backbone and defend what makes this country exceptional, we have real power — together, we keep proving that the American people will not give up our democracy without a fight. **How this chapter in history gets written is up to us — it depends on what we do in moments like this.[Make a donation today, and let’s rise to the occasion and fight for a truly representative democracy.](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/122145247/591751209/-1027206931?refcode=don_ndrc_tier1_email_AGEOYNote_email_20251228-NDRC-Tier1-AGEOYNote_&utm_source=email&utm_medium=email&utm_term=don&utm_content=20251228-NDRC-Tier1-AGEOYNote_&utm_campaign=AGEOYNote&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9FQS9FQTAxMy8xLzg5Mjk0IiwNCiAgIkRpc3RyaWJ1dGlvblVuaXF1ZUlkIjogIjljODRhNzE0LTVjZTQtZjAxMS04MTk1LTAwMGQzYTFkNThhYSIsDQogICJFbWFpbEFkZHJlc3MiOiAiZHB3aWxsaXM2N0BnbWFpbC5jb20iDQp9&hmac=gNIjIkWLtk6b5qeWXLv_FAa6fIvAFVuu_TJPxdX_Bvo=)** I’m honored to be with you on this side of history. In solidarity, Eric H. Holder, Jr.
82nd Attorney General of the United States

clean_body: If you take one lesson away from 2025, let it be this: | Peter, American democracy has been put through a gauntlet in 2025. It started with Republicans in North Carolina trying to overturn the result of a free and fair election for state supreme court. Thanks to people like you, democracy ultimately prevailed. Then powerful right-wing interests, including Elon Musk, spent millions to try to buy a seat on the Wisconsin Supreme Court and flip the balance of power. Our movement fought back, and won the day. But we continue to face existential, anti-democracy threats. Conservatives have petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court to effectively strike down the Voting Rights Act and upend the voting power of communities of color in America. We anxiously await that ruling. And throughout the last five months, Republicans have thrust the nation into a shameful redistricting crisis orchestrated by the Trump White House. They’re trying to rig the outcome of the midterm elections so they can’t lose. The ultimate outcome of their cynical power grab remains up in the air. A lot remains uncertain, but if you take one lesson away from the past year, let it be this: Some folks on the other side want you to believe they’re all-powerful. They want you to be dispirited and pessimistic about our future. But we’ve seen time and again that it’s a lie. When we organize, when we stand up for justice, when we show some backbone and defend what makes this country exceptional, we have real power — together, we keep proving that the American people will not give up our democracy without a fight. How this chapter in history gets written is up to us — it depends on what we do in moments like this.= I’m honored to be with you on this side of history. In solidarity, Eric H. Two of _Little House on the Prairie_ 's most famous sisters are [burying the hatchet](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFuwyAYhJ_G3ogAO9gZGLpkS9eOFphL-CsMFvxJlLevUqlP0PWkO933fV2Wi6NE-fbpNli-liXj2RKYUZdUfGPUCGrsKzG1uLvMpS1a6qNQWujTEhyl1zL2wV4BjaGHVZOZpDTDPPfRqnGc4R2wDrPzXkvvp1EqFcxpdKtbe7LvNaX1SSlptDk4rwZIZeYQpuMxrN0oEYhLPXwXyhxxTa_yQD2sZeuTjcx764aPTp87fcbzHXf6vCFRa07cKHlUFhX3TIwmEjEniFjuDaJkwRFir44qQTR6A4u_brtDuBxQW8lCqXkyxsi-2rA_KSVqZupGedscpd8v_C-BD6t_AgAA__-9cYgJ), as we report in _Etcetera_ below. ## Trump Meets Zelensky on Ukraine Peace
President Trump met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday to [discuss security guarantees for Ukraine](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFurDAQRb_GdCB7DAYKF6-h29emRAYPyyQGI3t2Efn6iPxC6ivdo3M-HuPDUaD9-d9taHmJ445nDsiMaQxxyoxpRco8JWLK6-F2jnkECU2poIR-9I7CNdaFtwsioC7Qqta0UhrddcVqlcKpM9Dior2be9k0upt772qNxteLL8jebwqgV0oaMJWblEapTOd92zR-FrVETxxT9Rlp5xWXcMU3pmqOWxHsynxkof8JGAQM53lW85Rvi3sXMAR6Y_k6vGPMAgZOr-0ovzHgnr-uq9wQmfZnuYSYyDsBQ5GsP04KgbJpRS2fm6PwC-M_FXpb-AkAAP__vC59Cg), hours after a "good and very productive" call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump said the two [are 90% agreed](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkL2u2zAMhZ9G3hRIdPyTwUMXb7drR4Oy6Gu2smRIdIK8faG8wt0OyIMP_Pjna_lCDhy_f-NBk2xpifQqgUQoLyG5IpR34iIus3DZT4ySygIGOm1Bw2PxyOG93Bs_bURAbUOTHfrBmL4dx2afvGtxw60zvnOrexDC5oa78avprevt2PBUaRbgYa3pob-hsy0Z24_eD13nV3U35FlSvv1NHGWnLbzTk_JtTUcTpl3kLKr9pWBWMMf3mYrUlYK5ghXMFmoeFcxX0dVPwSz5Ok794lDltSQtGZ8Uarr-ZeRI-mRZd31iDowHRdEp6pV87QeMvlbzVQqj5qgdfwYUvX5hVjA3efLnh1_6Qd3N94EcPifLj_78nOB_AAAA___iJJQX) on Zelensky's 20-point peace plan now under review by the Kremlin, though territorial issues in Donbas remain "very thorny," and suggested he'd be willing to travel to Ukraine to pitch parliament on ceding land to Russia. Russia launched [over 2,100 drones](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGurCAURb9GOwwcFbSgeI3dvPaVBuQ4njcIBpgx3q-_8f7CbfdOdvZa_x7zw5Cn8PxrdtRljXPAM3ssBdPso80F04aUi01UKG-HCSXmGTj0TACDcXaG_DV3tdMrImBboxZKKs5lOwz1phVKdL1SSlpUalQW-ODaQY0wWuxGU5O-1wTAKASXIBtjRYtcyME51fduqTqOjkpMzf9IoWy4-it-MDVL3Guvt1KOXLV_KpgqmM7zbIJdboq7v5OYvKtger-SoYAVTCW994N9oceQX9fFdsRC4clWHxM5w14XfdgWD8wsLcFAL8TY10m74yTvKUtVdfy5G_I_F8qvvH00fAcAAP__BPWD7w) and 94 missiles at Ukraine this week, with Saturday's assault alone killing two and wounding 27 while knocking out power in parts of Kyiv. Trump said peace is "closer than ever before" and plans to host Zelensky and European leaders in Washington next month.
## $400K Lobster Heist Exposes Cargo Theft Crisis
Thieves stole [$400,000 worth of lobsters](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOozAURb_GdI7sBzFQuNiGLttuiRz7Ed7G2Mh-ScTfjxjNH0x3pSsd3Xv-3eabo0jp8ddtaHnJc8JPjciMZY75XhnLilT5XoiprrtLnOsMCq5Sg4RxDo7iMXdNsAsiYNug1b3plTLtMDSr9Up574dh6R12qMEs7Tgq8C36YEY_NmRPmgYYtVYGzMXddYtKmyGE_noNXnQKA3Eul_-ZEq-4xCO_sVx83ppoV-a9ivaPgEnAlI49Vz4rAdMJFjBpOPMgYHpVef4TMPFK-MYqNxdQ5mWRH-JVdko9JSXpc2Wf5Y-AKl-V0kPWhO55nATJhfxTwNQUG_YPxUjV9KJTj81R_B7Gv7L5tvAVAAD__zpWiYI) bound for Costco stores in Illinois and Minnesota by impersonating legitimate carriers with spoofed emails and burner phones after picking up the shipment in Taunton, Massachusetts. Now that everyone has rage-clicked into this and is already halfway to the comments section or my inbox, let me explain what I actually mean when I say I support the school voucher idea/ethos.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/98559367-6171-4a99-85cf-0ab1c7e8e13c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Because what I am arguing for is not what either side usually thinks it is.
First, let's be clear about what school vouchers are.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..vAURuAjMmq0GYE_ugHKLZURnTj1C0uGGlvnvVRlskWc?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=182529222)
School vouchers, sometimes branded as "school choice," allow parents to send their children to a school other than their assigned public school. The tax dollars that would normally go to that public school instead follow the child to a private school. The pitch has always been the same. Escape poorly run districts. Increase competition. Improve outcomes.
In practice, what vouchers really do is take a pool of public money meant for communal goods and redirect it to private institutions. Sometimes nonprofit. Sometimes explicitly for-profit.
That alone should already tell you something important.
I do not support sending public money to private institutions. Taxpayer dollars should fund communal services that benefit everyone. If a service does not benefit the public broadly, it should not be publicly funded.
Yes, there are exceptions. Research grants. Gap-filling nonprofits. Specific, measurable public benefit. Those should be evaluated individually, with accountability and transparency.
And yes, I have a problem with nonprofit executives making half a million dollars a year off taxpayer-adjacent funding. That is not charity. That is rent-seeking with better branding.
So no, my support for vouchers is not about privatizing education.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/4b07d643-9217-4581-9d7d-d2d28526afaf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
### The Problem Is School Boundaries
Here is the part people refuse to talk about honestly.
School boundaries function as one of the most powerful and quiet forms of gatekeeping in this country.
If you are born into a bad school district, or your parents cannot afford to move, that is it. That decision is made for you. Your zip code becomes destiny.
That is insane.
[Share The Angry Democrat](https://substack.com/redirect/69d601e3-9b16-4458-9aa2-93a1299ae650?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
If your child is strong in STEM but your assigned school has a good football program, why is that child locked out of a public school across town with a top science program?
If your child is a gifted athlete and your district does not invest in that sport, why is there no pathway to a public school that does?
We already accept competition everywhere else in education. Colleges compete. Students apply. Programs differentiate. Resources follow talent and demand.
Why do we treat K-12 education like a static utility instead of a dynamic system?
#### Let me be clear about something people keep misunderstanding.
I do **not** support opting out of paying for public schools. Schools are a public good and it is about contributing to communities and sharing the common good.
If you have all-electric appliances, should you ask why you are paying for gas lines? If you are blind, should you ask why you are paying for filling potholes in roads you can't drive on? If you hate technology, should you ask why we are laying fiber optic cable?
Schools draw more heat because they are expensive and because not everyone has kids in the system at the same time. I understand that instinct.
But schools are not just classrooms.
They raise property values. They anchor communities. They host elections. They serve seniors. They create stability that benefits everyone, whether you have kids or not.
So no, this is not an argument to stop paying for public education.
The real problem is worse.
We force everyone to pay in, and then we lock kids into school boundaries that decide their future based on zip code. You cannot opt out, and you cannot meaningfully opt into something better either.
### Public Schools Should Compete With Other Public Schools
What I support is competition within the public school system.
Tax dollars should follow students between public schools. Not private schools. And before you start yelling, "this is open enrollment," open enrollment is completely voluntary from district to district, with different enrollment windows. Almost all districts in my area don't even have open enrollment. If you DO want to call this open enrollment, then open enrollment should be mandatory.
I think it should go like this.
If a public school can educate two thousand students safely and responsibly but only has fourteen hundred enrolled, those six hundred empty seats should be opened up. Obviously priority to the kids in the school district. But after they are enrolled the remainder of the seats opens up.
**Those unused seats are public capacity.**
Those seats represent revenue. Resources. Opportunity. The redistribution of your tax dollars.
Schools should be allowed to specialize. Arts. Trades. STEM. Literature. Athletics. They should compete to be excellent at something instead of mediocre at everything.
Students should apply. Not just enroll automatically.
That does not mean open enrollment chaos. It means standards. Grades. Behavior. Fit. Schools should be allowed to reject applicants, with clear explanations for why.
Yes, parents will be angry. That is not a reason to avoid the system. That is how college works. Merit matters. Fit matters. Accountability matters.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..vAURuAjMmq0GYE_ugHKLZURnTj1C0uGGlvnvVRlskWc?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=182529222)
### What About the Schools That Lose Students
This is where people panic.
If some schools lose students and funding, what happens?
Here is the uncomfortable answer. They consolidate.
If two schools with one thousand students each now have seven hundred apiece, combine them. You get a stronger fourteen-hundred-student school with more resources, better programs, and more focused investment.
Right now, we treat school districts like sacred geography. Fixed. Untouchable. Immovable.
That mindset locks failure in place and insulates class barriers.
If a district is bad and cannot attract students, how exactly is it supposed to improve under the current system? More money alone does not fix institutional rot. Incentives do.
### Yes, This Threatens Gatekeeping. That's the Point.
Let's be honest about the real objections.
**NIMBY** : Not in my backyard.
The same argument used against affordable housing or multifamily housing gets deployed here. We do not want _**those**_ kids/people in our schools. They will bring crime. They will lower standards. They will change the culture.
That fear says more about the people expressing it than about the kids.
If you want to send your child to a private school to avoid that discomfort, fine. Pay for it yourself.
Public schools should serve the public.
Now, people will scream about equity.
What if poor kids cannot get transportation? Offer it where possible. But no, it does not need to be an absolute requirement.
What if they do not fit in? Their clothes are cheaper. Their parents do not buy them cars.
Welcome to life.
Teach kids humility. Teach empathy. Teach your privileged kids not to be assholes. This is not a policy failure. This is parenting.
If being exposed to wealth disparities is uncomfortable, maybe that discomfort is educational. Maybe... it may... wait for it... create empathy.
### Religion and Identity in Schools
A lot of parents choose private schools for religious reasons. I understand that.
But we have also stripped so much individuality out of public schools that the only identities left are consumerism and social class.
We say separation of church and state, but what we often mean is sterilization of community culture. We can respect pluralism without turning schools into ideological voids.
That said, if you want a religious education, go to a religious school and pay for it.
### The Real Issue Is Zip Code Destiny
The single strongest predictor of upward mobility in this country is zip code.
That is not merit. That is not character. That is not work ethic.
That is structural inequality baked into geography.
If we are serious about giving kids real opportunity, we have to break the link between where they are born and what they are allowed to become.
Allowing students to move between public schools is the cleanest first step.
### The Bottom Line
I support a voucher-like system inside public education.
Public dollars should follow students between public schools. Schools should compete. Students should apply. Excellence should be rewarded. Failure should not be protected indefinitely.
If you are a progressive who claims to care about equity, or a conservative who claims to care about merit, this should not scare you.
And if it does, ask yourself why.
Disagree with me. Argue with me. But do not pretend the current system is fair, functional, or moral.

## Father Rescues Kidnapped Daughter
A Montgomery County father [rescued his 15-year-old](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0L2SsyAUBuCrwQ6HH6OhoPgau3ztls4RDsIsEQcwJne_Y3Znb2Dr8zPv837cphuEGNblP9xR16dL04pHiVgr5slB9ZgzFrNj-Qx2hW1Da2GfBBMXygUVarIQ4mvqGqtnZhVvUPOhHxhT_XBtvGbKmV50M84zm1kn-wHMVfXmcpFGWS6boM9nXAjFBeN8aJ0D1klrpZLApEHSMbShptxWjxWfUFx8pQfm1qR7E7WvdStE_iNiJGI8jqN16XkqzjkR416IGN939BtEf0T0l0Qt7IuvmGnNYMK60HNt82nFQmMyUENaafGYg3OFJueCQVrgVZqs7XaEGEPpB9Kx5Q4hvoPVv9X50OIrAAD__5QzjkQ) daughter after she was kidnapped on Christmas while walking her dog. The man found her about two miles from her family's home in Porter by [tracking her phone's location](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkD2O5CAQhU-DM1pQYGMHDjZxNptuaFVTRRs1_hHg8cztV945wmZVetLT-74_H_MHxhS3129ceaxfYZ83vkriWjnPAevCOXPxJ5d3pA2Pg4nwnEFBKzVIGGbCmL5n29D4VDTohkftOqfU0Lm-WUajfBdU39qu7W1rDbW6ZT_0OhB5DKGJ412mAQYNSmv3CAGVNURmMKiMZ2EVU6x7ftSFK39hCel7_-T88PvapHGp9SjC_BIwCZiu63q8l_28QwET5hp9YgHTzSVg8jmu9_vDJo9l31jWjP4dt5dMu8fK8odVEp6vpXKW5SwH-yrxllGZBEzQt9LpFtGZ-9AgrSMnnzoYqYzprSMLz-fQ5JGOK6YUS-eEVa8VY_q3vP6f788R_gYAAP__ecqTwg). Authorities were called to the scene, and 23-year-old Giovanni Rosales Espinoza was arrested without incident. Espinoza allegedly threatened the girl [with a knife](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLGyozAMRb_GdM4YQeJQuNiG7m27JSMsETxxbMYWj-Tvd9jZP3idCs2599w_X9MXhhjS4ze-2Ml7yVPio0YW4TItKCuXwtXvXJ-BEm4bE-E-gYGrbkHDMBGG-Jn6htxsaGgbdq29WWOGm703q_Mz2RnmO8LQA1PPnu6zMban7mq6KzXBnbAWYGjBtK29LAuaviPqhg5N51n1hilILhdZWfiNdYmf_M3l4vOriW4V2arqfikYFYzHcVx8DP4Ja96r5HR-KRhPLQVjzB6jgvHMVDC2cN5WwVj3urEXjaevMGlchIv-bx3SQwtz0o9QokbRzxQW3nJIol--Zl3xc-Kb4mg7Qoyh3qzqzeOFIf7rKT9b99vB3wAAAP__Fc-QRg) and drove her to a secluded area. He is charged with aggravated kidnapping and indecency with a child. "_Christmas is a day meant for joy, but this man chose to shatter that joy by targeting a child_ ," [said Sheriff Wesley Doolittle](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL1uhDAQhJ8GOiN7zU8oXKShu7Qp0R67gHUGI9uc794-IsobpJ7RaL7v-zbe0Dq7L1-4sUmv2Y875-g4JQ7jjGnlEDhOJ8eHpR2Pg4nwHEFCIxQI6EdC695jXZK5S-pVyUZ1bSdl33Yf5WpaqTRiQ6hwlrqdWHfEoJquVXc94b205hpTAL0CqVRXzTPKWhPpXqPUExe1ZLLJhyqtnPiFcXZv_-RQTX4rnVlTOmKhPwsYChhyztXsX9Cu_ozJ71epgOGiKmA4fEgcxIa7wGk6I5P447L7IhYbnFCNyKt1LOLKImMUGd3jSskvZTB0ZOucjW1X1HLZ0LrfG-l_8p4GfgIAAP__XBKGcA) in a statement. "_I am incredibly proud of our deputies and detectives who worked tirelessly to ensure this dangerous predator was swiftly apprehended and is now off our streets_."
## Facility Spills 1M Gallons of Sulfuric Acid
A storage tank at a Houston facility released about [1 million gallons of sulfuric acid](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL2S2zAMhJ-G6ughob-oUJFG3aVNqcER0BFzsKghacvO02eUV0i3xc5-u_v7Y_1AUdm_fuGd5_ra0rrzWZRr5bxuWCPnzCU8uHwL7XgcTISPFRz01oOFaSUUfa9dQ_Ono8k3PPtxGJ2bhvFHE-et7R221Id-6lzbDUM_dJN3NHZI_WegRuYrzANMHpz3423b0HUtUTu16NrApnNMUlO-1ciVX1g2facn51tI90bnWOtRTPvTwGJgOc_zFlTCN8T0KDXtl8vAcs0ysGgKqAaWi2lg8XDp0cASIu4761P4tCHyXQKqLYeo2pD2irIzWbAxlUMqqvxhsqfUaDOXQzLWlN9WSnnwhWnyTMcpqlKG0XTu646i__rW_3v5OcPfAAAA___hXZLy) on Saturday after an overhead walkway fell onto it. Two people were hospitalized with respiratory difficulty but have since been released, while another 44 were medically evaluated on-site. The incident occurred around 1:40 a.m. at a facility operated by Houston-based BWC Terminals. According to the company, most of the acid in the 25,000-barrel storage tank was contained at the facility, though an [undetermined amount](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJyk0b2unDAQBeCngW5WtvlbCopt6G6KKEpKNGuPF-sOBtnD5fL2ESvlCVJ_ozk6On8-pg8MHOLrBy40yLdfp0hHZhKhNHmUmVKibHfKn8FF3DZyDvfJKNOANmD6yWHgc6pLNzyV63VJg-7aTqm-7e7lPNino2evfdPevUbVOKxs01Jf0b122rZlGK5n2pheG6V1d_MeVV05V_UVqspSUStyQdZ0k5mEvjF7PtcvSje7LiUPs8iWi-pRmLEw43EctyXHywozUoQ9F2bc9icHCxk9yQkYHdBC6UXRBrp8JmSZ3_DvhinJRRqWwBzWCC9kXmOG1UPe2e8pWEAbHCRiwkwO0AslOJA_DzzBrsy4ZcqAAoRZYMaUQga77lFO2BijFGbEBI-H_nVvfv8s0-C248rLbVfU6rVg4HdP-b91vgbzNwAA__-XD6nO) entered the Houston Ship Channel. Air quality monitoring indicated there is [no ongoing threat](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkL2SnDAQhJ9GZNrSDD9aAgVOyM6pQ2rQjA55tYgSWrh7e9feKzjuqu7-vj8f8wfFFLfP3_QUV79Cnje5jiS1SpkD1VVKkcO_5HhE3mjfhZleMxrsNaDGcWaK6XvuGnaL4REacWAHa8w42HuzumXse6AOAIwxHS898QhAwdoAwHffRPcuA8QR0ADYWwhkupa5HVsyrRfVGeFYc7nVVap80RHSdz6l3Hx-Nsmtte6Han8pnBRO13XdHmt-vUOFE5UafRKF05tL4ZSyp6Rw-ks-bjXvuVS95FeSkwprv8ozeko6CT20X2nbJJ1RLv0zrHDCe69tG9oBe6_7BUh3ZmA9Mtw1WmmRCAdk0xTH-xVTisdgVWc-nxTTz-P6f55Ph_8CAAD__4fHkNk) to the surrounding area. Harris County Judge Lina Hidalgo said authorities would "conduct a full investigation to ensure transparency and accountability."
## A&M Team Develops AI-Powered Robotic Dog
A team of Texas A&M University engineering students developed an [AI-powered robotic dog](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkD1uoDAQRk8DnZFt_gsX29Bl2y3R4BnAirGRPQS4_Sq5QspPn_T09P59zB_gvAvbXzjI8LPGOdCdPTFTmlfgnVKibC_Knw4DnCchwjVrqVuhtNDjjOD8OzclmkXiqEoyqu96KceuH8rdtLppO2oXOw6ghqFG6LCxukYCCV1PpTPfMKX1qLRUqq_WFWRTI9ZjDbK2VDSS0HFMFe_E9EBe_Ru_KFU2HqU3O_OZi_pPoadCT_d9V58PhO-z0BOT3UP0cXt_xgNZwCEobC4QJRc2kflCCpzFcjmPIsUlsrMCnDjjTYlQYNwER7GTP8XteBd0UNoo2FckymcMmQo9lcngeTvvXe76opHbAc7_KPLvwn4Z_T8AAP__O16Rpg) that could aid in disaster response and search-and-rescue operations. The prototype uses a camera input and navigation system to identify objects and plan routes in hard-to-access areas. It can [remember where it's been](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkD2OpDAYRE8DGS3bQAOBg03IetMNkcFl82mNjeyv_24_6pkjTFhS6T3p_bstN0OBov9rDmh-ubREPEsAM_LiDO_IGWW7o_wnG815wlpzX5RQfSNVo6bFGgrvpautXoWdZA0th-sgxHQdxnrXctqMdGpsx3XrIR0wKtf1_Yq-H7q1q0l_YFKpSSoh5XBxzoiutbadWiPaDVUnYIlTvvAOxssUF97pgXzZ0lEHvTOfpWr_VGqu1EyRkVGYokf0FIFM0X-ulZoNNTmtiWkrlZrv5Wc1NvkGB7JH3N5NRjlTLGgY5qiztueTQqByHapO-MNQ-Bbz73I9tPoKAAD__7MHgm0), adapt to changing environments, and receive voice commands. | | Friends,
As we approach the New Year, I want to take a moment to reflect on the road we have traveled together and where we are headed next.
The last five months have felt like a whirlwind. In that time, I have:

* Visited 65 counties
* Attended more than 125 campaign events
* Made over 1,200 calls to delegates
* Logged more than 30,000 miles on my vehicles

That mileage even came with a new transmission and catalytic converter, but that is what happens when you commit fully to meeting people where they are, all across our state.
None of this would be possible without my family, especially my wife Mina and my son Nic, whose support makes this work possible. I am also grateful to the entire team at TBG for their dedication and professionalism.
Most importantly, I want to thank the delegates, county parties, and district leaders who have welcomed me, offered guidance, and placed their trust in this campaign. I am especially thankful for the endorsements I have received so far. Each one is meaningful, and I do not take that support lightly.
As we look ahead to 2026, my commitment is simple: to continue showing up, listening, and earning your trust. I welcome your calls, your questions, and your feedback, and I encourage you to reach out anytime. If you believe in the direction of this campaign, I would be honored to earn your endorsement as well.
There is more work to do, and I am energized by what lies ahead.
I hope you had a very Merry Christmas and a blessed holiday season, and I wish you and your families a happy, healthy, and successful New Year.
Sincerely,
Doug Lloyd Eaton County Prosecuting Attorney Candidate for Michigan Attorney General

Happy New Year's Eve! Next week I'm going to have predictions for '26, but right now it's a bit of reflection on the year that was.
2025 was... a year. For me, it was very good. Everyone stayed healthy. We launched [Noble Mobile](https://substack.com/redirect/f850c477-9de4-4278-908a-4f88015c90eb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), which has been a joy. It's great building something that both saves people money and gets them off their screens a bit (17% reduction in screen time for early users!). Thousands of people have come to [Offline](https://substack.com/redirect/6884a615-2911-4e14-a3b8-cc8ba8f445bf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) parties, which have taken on a life of their own. I finished a [book](https://substack.com/redirect/3377a590-32cb-4626-a0b2-6c6c3f523188?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) I'm excited to have out. The year has been productive and generative.
But out there, it seemed like a gross year. Troubling headlines abounded. People feel unsettled. The AI boom has most people shaking their heads about the future. The vibes were bad.
I asked people on social media, "How was 2025 for you?" 30% said "Okay" and 23% answered "Poor / bad / terrible." That seems representative.
How do we measure how things are going? A recent Wall Street Journal poll gauged what Americans agreed were very important. The results were jarring; Americans have gotten markedly less interested in patriotism, religion, having children, or community involvement.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/15a07c7b-23b8-42f9-95f1-f2db000399ab?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
You know the only thing that is going up that people agree is 'very important to them'? Money.
Yikes. But in a way it's unsurprising.
What makes a society more likely to focus on money? In my view, it's a mindset of scarcity, where you feel like if you don't have a certain amount of money, you can't afford a good life.
Look, I get it. These things are real. I've felt for years that the easiest, most straightforward way to improve people's lives at scale is to put money into their hands. And if someone asks you 'how was your year?', the first thing you might think about is your bank account or your kitchen table. You doing better financially? Probably been a good year. You struggling financially? Probably a tough one.
That said, I've always felt the bottom line was about more than that. I made a number of choices in my younger years that were financially unwise. I wanted to be a good person, whatever that meant, and do interesting, impactful work, whatever that meant. If you ask me what the best thing I could do for a person is, it would be to connect them with a role or a great opportunity that brings out the best in them and allows them to grow. That is the stuff of magic.
Social media has substituted a different form of currency for a lot of people; if you're a teenager at home, what's the most valuable type of affirmation you can receive? Likes on a post or picture you've put up by your peers. It makes you feel admired and important. And if you get enough of those likes, maybe you can convert them to money eventually, too. There's now an entire industry defined by this that has shaped the aspirations of millions.
I'm glad I came to social media as an adult who grew up in the 70s, 80s, and 90s before everything went digital. I had a fully formed brain.
Happiness scholar Arthur Brooks came on the podcast recently, and he talks a lot about the meaning of life and how to be happy. You know what's not on his menu? Financial advice. He talks about having something sacred in your life, and trying to follow the right goals. "The problem is that striving for happiness directly, in the abstract, is not possible. Instead you must choose proxy goals: metaphorical stars in the sky that you can see and judge to lead you to the greater well-being you desire."
So how do you choose good goals? Arthur, very helpfully, has a few tips:
1\. Focus on people, not things. It turns out, if there's a three-word shorthand for the science of happiness: happiness is love.
2\. It's about you and your inner direction, not about how others see you. Social comparison and happiness are negatively correlated.
3\. Make a happy journey your goal, too. Arriving at a destination doesn't generally keep you joyous for long, so you need to enjoy the trip.
To which he adds a fourth:
4\. Stay flexible and be ready to find another way. Things change. Feel free to change too.
This feels like much more satisfying, nuanced advice than "pad your bank account," though that can of course be part of the goals that you set. Happiness is other people. In real life. Doing things that are meaningful to them. Let's do more of that in the New Year.
Happy New Year! "Fix it in '26."
\- Andrew

Next week I'm going to have predictions for '26, but right now it's a bit of reflection on the year that was. 2025 was... a year. For me, it was very good. Everyone stayed healthy. We launched , which has been a joy. It's great building something that both saves people money and gets them off their screens a bit (17% reduction in screen time for early users!). Thousands of people have come to parties, which have taken on a life of their own. I finished a I'm excited to have out. The year has been productive and generative. But out there, it seemed like a gross year. Troubling headlines abounded. People feel unsettled. The AI boom has most people shaking their heads about the future. The vibes were bad. I asked people on social media, "How was 2025 for you?" 30% said "Okay" and 23% answered "Poor / bad / terrible." That seems representative. How do we measure how things are going? A recent Wall Street Journal poll gauged what Americans agreed were very important. I've felt for years that the easiest, most straightforward way to improve people's lives at scale is to put money into their hands. And if someone asks you 'how was your year?', the first thing you might think about is your bank account or your kitchen table. You doing better financially? Probably been a good year. There's now an entire industry defined by this that has shaped the aspirations of millions. I'm glad I came to social media as an adult who grew up in the 70s, 80s, and 90s before everything went digital. I had a fully formed brain. | | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

If you have ever held a magnifying glass up to the teachings of today's far Christian Right, you may have noticed a stark departure from the traditional teachings of Christianity. Where charity and service were once emphasized, they have increasingly been replaced by a "winner-take-all" prosperity gospel under the guise of the American Dream--tragically and ironically fitting for a hyper-capitalistic society like the United States. Their mantra is simple: _" God helps those who help themselves."_
It is a faith rooted in the belief that no matter how wealth is acquired, it is inherently God's plan for you to have it--even if it comes at the expense of your fellow human beings--and that no one has the right to take it away. Charity and good works are at best optional. It is your divine right to hoard as much wealth as possible because, as one of their for-profit prophets, Norman Vincent Peale, once stated, "Empty pockets never held anyone back--only empty heads and empty hearts."
It is no coincidence that this theology is embraced most enthusiastically by wealthy billionaires, right-wing politicians, and the conmen who orbit them in and around Washington. It has been carefully manufactured to justify widening wealth inequality and the political and legislative decisions that reinforce it. After all, if God has ordained the outcome, how can anyone argue with it?
From trickle-down economics to tariffs, Republican economic strategies over the past half-century have frequently been coated in the holy veneer of evangelical Christianity--framed as helping others while overwhelmingly enriching those at the top. The prosperity gospel also fueled decades of "hustle and grind" grifts through multi-level marketing schemes, with companies like Amway and Mary Kay opening conventions with prayer so attendees might continue to be "blessed" with wealth from above.
The logical conclusion of this theological movement is--of course--its newest religious text: _Project 2025_ , which is now informing the policy direction of the current administration as it moves to strip food assistance, health care access, and retirement security from millions of Americans. The underlying logic is simple: I should only have to help myself, not others, because my faith tells me that wealth is next to holiness.
So how the hell did we get here--and how is this shaping our politics? If you'll join me, let's take our fourth deep dive into the fantastical world of far-right evangelical Christianity.
